reconcile.connective: Defenders distinguish prophesying under inspiration (permitted) from teaching with authority over men (restricted) as two separate categories, not one rule overriding the other.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman argues 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 was inserted later, since it flatly contradicts Paul's own assumption elsewhere that women pray and prophesy aloud in church.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: "The Silencing of Women: 1 Cor. 14:34-35 as an Interpolation," The Bart Ehrman Blog
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, "The Silencing of Women: 1 Cor. 14:34-35 as an Interpolation," The Bart Ehrman Blog (2024)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The relationship between teaching and authority depends on how both are understood. Women did teach (Titus 2:3-5), but there are no clear New Testament examples or endorsements of women teaching men in church meetings (cp. Acts 18:26; 1 Cor 14:34-35; Phil 4:3). We know it was happening in some of the churches only by way of Paul's opposing responses. Women did prophesy (Acts 2:17-18; 21:9; 1 Cor 11:5), but some types of prophecy might not have been seen as authoritative teaching (Acts 11:28; 21:10-11; 1 Cor 14:29).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly reconciles the row's core tension by distinguishing prophesying (permitted, and citing Acts 2:17-18 and 21:9 - both cited in this contradiction) from teaching-with-authority (restricted), explaining why the Deborah/prophesying texts don't override 1 Tim 2:12 / 1 Cor 14:34.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), pp. 308-310
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley sets this exact contradiction out in parallel columns - 'Should be in subjection' (Gen 3:16, 1 Cor 11:3, 1 Cor 14:34, Eph 5:22-24, 1 Pet 3:5-6) against 'May bear rule' / 'May prophesy and teach' (Judges 4:4-5,14 Deborah, Acts 2:18, Acts 18:26, Acts 21:9, 1 Cor 11:5) - then argues Paul's silence rules were local and situational (addressed to Corinth's and Ephesus's specific circumstances), not a universal, timeless prohibition.
